name: Kolb Experiential Learning Modes (Likert-adapted)
description: 12-item Likert adaptation of Kolb's Experiential Learning Theory, measuring four learning modes that combine into the four Kolb learning styles. Concrete Experience + Reflective Observation = Diverging; Abstract Conceptualization + Reflective Observation = Assimilating; Abstract Conceptualization + Active Experimentation = Converging; Concrete Experience + Active Experimentation = Accommodating. As with VARK, the empirical evidence for matching instruction to learning style is weak.
citation: Kolb, D. A. (1984). Experiential Learning: Experience as the Source of Learning and Development. Prentice-Hall. (Items rewritten in Likert form for this study; the original LSI uses a ranked-choice format.)
license: Kolb LSI © Hay Group; items rewritten in Likert form for this study (CC-BY).

dimensions.label: Concrete Experience
dimensions.description: Learning through feeling — engaging with concrete situations and people

dimensions.label: Reflective Observation
dimensions.description: Learning through watching — observing carefully before judging

dimensions.label: Abstract Conceptualization
dimensions.description: Learning through thinking — building models and theories

dimensions.label: Active Experimentation
dimensions.description: Learning through doing — practical application and testing

items.text: I learn best by getting personally involved in a situation and noticing my own reactions.
Before drawing conclusions, I prefer to step back and observe a situation from many angles.
I build mental models and theories to make sense of what I am learning.
I learn most when I can try something out and see what happens.
Feelings and intuition are an important part of how I understand things.
I prefer to listen and observe carefully before forming an opinion.
Abstract concepts and frameworks excite me more than concrete details.
I'd rather take action and learn from outcomes than analyze indefinitely.
I value direct, lived experience as my main source of learning.
Reflection — looking back over what happened — is essential to how I learn.
I enjoy precise logical analysis and reasoning from first principles.
Practical application is the real test of whether I've learned something.
